## Simple explanation

Inference is when a trained model uses new input to make a prediction or
generate an output. A spam filter labeling a new email and a language model
writing a response are both doing inference.

## Technical explanation

During inference, a model applies its learned parameters to input data to
produce predictions, scores, or generated sequences. Unlike training,
inference normally does not update those parameters. It may run locally,
in a server, or on an accelerator, and can process one request at a time
or a batch of requests.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Inference is the point where model behavior becomes part of a product or
workflow. Engineers must manage latency, throughput, memory, hardware cost,
reliability, and the quality of preprocessing and postprocessing.

## How it works

An inference path typically validates and preprocesses an input, loads or
calls the trained model, computes its output, and formats the result for
the application. Deployment choices include batching, quantization, and
hardware acceleration. Inference does not by itself guarantee that the
output is correct or safe for its intended use.

## Practical example

A deployed image classifier receives an uploaded photo, resizes and
normalizes it as expected by the model, computes class scores, and returns
a label and confidence information to the application.

## Common misconceptions

- Inference is not the same as training: ordinary inference uses learned
  parameters without updating them.
- Generative inference may involve many sequential model steps, not just
  one prediction.
- A model's confidence score is not automatically a calibrated probability
  or a guarantee of correctness.
